text: Complete ReactJS Made Simple Every topic explained with a picture you will never forget + a working code example How to use these notes 1. Read the story - it is the picture that sticks. 2. Type the code in a Vite project (see topic 2). Never copy-paste. 3. Say the REMEMBER line out loud. 4. Next day, rebuild the example from memory. Before React, know these JavaScript tools let/const, arrow functions, template literals, destructuring, spread (...), map / filter / reduce, ES modules (import / export), promises and async/await. If any feel shaky, revise them first - React is mostly just JavaScript.

Complete ReactJS Made Simple - page 3 PART 1 - REACT BASICS 1. What is React and Why Use It? React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces out of Lego bricks called components. You describe WHAT the screen should look like for the current data, and React updates the page for you (declarative). It keeps a light copy of the page (the Virtual DOM), compares old vs new, and changes only what differs - fast and tidy. // Without React (imperative): you give every step const p = document.createElement("p"); p.textContent = "Count: " + count; document.body.appendChild(p); // With React (declarative): you describe the result function Counter({ count }) { return

Count: {count}

; } // When count changes, React updates only that text for you. REMEMBER: React = components (Lego bricks) + state. You describe the UI, React updates it. 2. Setting Up with Vite Vite is the modern,

Setting Up with Vite Vite is the modern, fast tool that creates a ready React project. You need Node.js installed first. # In the terminal: npm create vite@latest my-app -- --template react cd my-app npm install npm run dev # open http://localhost:5173 # Folder map # index.html the single page # src/main.jsx starts React (the entry point) # src/App.jsx your first component # package.json list of packages and scripts // src/main.jsx import { createRoot } from "react-dom/client"; import App from "./App"; createRoot(document.getElementById("root")).render(<App />); REMEMBER: npm create vite, npm install, npm run dev. main.jsx plugs App into #root.

Complete ReactJS Made Simple - page 8 PART 2 - STATE AND HOOKS (THE HEART OF REACT) 11. useState: Giving a Component Memory State is the component's memory, like a whiteboard. Change the whiteboard with the setter function and React re-draws the screen. Normal variables are forgotten on every render - state is remembered. import { useState } from "react"; function Counter() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); // [value, setter] = initial value return (

Count: {count}

{/* safe form */}
); } // Never do: count = count + 1; (React will not notice!) REMEMBER: const [value, setValue] = useState(start). Call setValue to update and redraw. 12. State Rules: Never Mutate, Always Replace React only notices when you hand it a new object or array, like giving the

= useState(start). Call setValue to update and redraw. 12. State Rules: Never Mutate, Always Replace React only notices when you hand it a new object or array, like giving the teacher a fresh answer sheet instead of scribbling on the old one. Use spread, map and filter to make copies. const [user, setUser] = useState({ name: "Asha", age: 20 }); const [todos, setTodos] = useState(["Learn React"]); // Objects: copy, then override setUser({ ...user, age: 21 }); // NOT user.age = 21 // Arrays setTodos([...todos, "Build app"]); // add setTodos(todos.filter(t => t !== "Learn React")); // remove setTodos(todos.map(t => t === "x" ? "y" : t)); // update one // Updating from the previous value (batching-safe) setCount(prev => prev + 1); // State updates are asynchronous: the new value shows on the NEXT render // setCount(5); console.log(count); // still the old value here REMEMBER: Replace, don't mutate: spread for objects, map/filter

// State updates are asynchronous: the new value shows on the NEXT render // setCount(5); console.log(count); // still the old value here REMEMBER: Replace, don't mutate: spread for objects, map/filter for arrays.

Complete ReactJS Made Simple - page 9 13. Lifting State Up When two siblings need the same data, move the state to their closest common parent and pass it down as props. Like keeping the scoreboard in the middle of the stadium where everyone can see. function Parent() { const [text, setText] = useState(""); // state lives HERE return ( <> ); } function Input({ value, onChange }) { return onChange(e.target.value)} />; } function Preview({ value }) { return

You typed: {value}

; } REMEMBER: Shared data lives in the parent. Data goes down, events go up. 14. Controlled Inputs and Forms A controlled input gets its value from state, so React is always in charge, like a teacher holding the class register. function SignUp() { const [form, setForm] = useState({ name: "", email: "", agree: false }); function

state, so React is always in charge, like a teacher holding the class register. function SignUp() { const [form, setForm] = useState({ name: "", email: "", agree: false }); function handleChange(e) { const { name, value, type, checked } = e.target; setForm({ ...form, [name]: type === "checkbox" ? checked : value }); } function handleSubmit(e) { e.preventDefault(); // stop page reload console.log("Submitted:", form); } return ( <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}> <input name="name" value={form.name} onChange={handleChange} /> <input name="email" value={form.email} onChange={handleChange} /> <input name="agree" type="checkbox" checked={form.agree} onChange={handleChange} /> <button disabled={!form.agree}>Join</button> </form> ); } REMEMBER: value={state} + onChange={update} = controlled input. One handler with [name].

Complete ReactJS Made Simple - page 10 15. useEffect: Doing Things After Render Effects are for side-effects: things outside rendering such as fetching data, timers, changing the page title. The dependency array decides when to run: [] = once, [x] = when x changes, none = every render. import { useState, useEffect } from "react"; function Demo() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); useEffect(() => { // runs once after first render console.log("Component appeared"); }, []); useEffect(() => { // runs when count changes document.title = `Count: ${count}`; }, [count]); return <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>{count}</button>; } // Think: "After render, if these values changed, do this." REMEMBER: useEffect(fn, [deps]): [] once, [x] when x changes. 16. useEffect Cleanup If an effect starts something (timer, listener, connection), return a cleanup function to switch it off - like turning off the tap when you leave. function Clock() { const [time,

If an effect starts something (timer, listener, connection), return a cleanup function to switch it off - like turning off the tap when you leave. function Clock() { const [time, setTime] = useState(new Date().toLocaleTimeString()); useEffect(() => { const id = setInterval(() => { setTime(new Date().toLocaleTimeString()); }, 1000); return () => clearInterval(id); // cleanup when component leaves }, []); return

{time}

; } function WindowSize() { const [w, setW] = useState(window.innerWidth); useEffect(() => { const onResize = () => setW(window.innerWidth); window.addEventListener("resize", onResize); return () => window.removeEventListener("resize", onResize); }, []); return

Width: {w}

; } REMEMBER: Start something in an effect? Return a function that stops it.

Complete ReactJS Made Simple - page 11 17. useRef: A Box That Does Not Redraw useRef is a sticky note that survives re-renders, but changing it does NOT redraw the screen. Two main uses: grab a DOM element, or keep a value (timer id, previous value). import { useRef, useEffect } from "react"; function FocusInput() { const inputRef = useRef(null); useEffect(() => { inputRef.current.focus(); // touch the real DOM element }, []); return <input ref={inputRef} placeholder="I get focus automatically" />; } function Stopwatch() { const timerId = useRef(null); // remembers value, no re-render const start = () => { timerId.current = setInterval(() => console.log("tick"), 1000); }; const stop = () => clearInterval(timerId.current); return <><button onClick={start}>Start</button><button onClick={stop}>Stop</button></>; } REMEMBER: useRef = DOM access or a silent memory. ref.current holds the value. 18. useContext: Skipping the Prop Chain Passing props through 5 levels is like passing a note through 5 people. Context

DOM access or a silent memory. ref.current holds the value. 18. useContext: Skipping the Prop Chain Passing props through 5 levels is like passing a note through 5 people. Context is a loudspeaker: any component below can listen directly. Great for theme, logged-in user, language. import { createContext, useContext, useState } from "react"; const ThemeContext = createContext("light"); // 1. create function ThemeProvider({ children }) { // 2. provide const [theme, setTheme] = useState("light"); return ( <ThemeContext.Provider value={{ theme, setTheme }}> {children} </ThemeContext.Provider> ); } function ThemeButton() { // 3. use anywhere below const { theme, setTheme } = useContext(ThemeContext); return ( <button onClick={() => setTheme(theme === "light" ? "dark" : "light")}> Now: {theme} </button> ); } // Wrap the app: <ThemeProvider><App /></ThemeProvider> REMEMBER: createContext -> Provider value -> useContext. No more prop drilling.

Complete ReactJS Made Simple - page 12 19. useReducer: State with Rules When state has many actions, use a reducer: a manager that takes the current state plus an action (a request slip) and returns the new state. Like a bank teller handling deposit/withdraw slips. import { useReducer } from "react"; function reducer(state, action) { switch (action.type) { case "add": return [...state, { id: Date.now(), text: action.text }]; case "remove": return state.filter(t => t.id !== action.id); case "clear": return []; default: return state; } } function Todos() { const [todos, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, []); return ( <> {todos.map(t => (

dispatch({ type: "remove", id: t.id })}> {t.text}

))} ); } REMEMBER: dispatch(action) -> reducer(state, action) -> new state.

{/* no re-filter */} setQuery(e.target.value)} /> {filtered.map(p =>

{p.name}

value. 21. useCallback and React.memo React.memo says 'skip re-drawing this child if props are the same'. But a function made inside a parent is new on every render, so props look different. useCallback keeps the same function, so memo works. import { memo, useCallback, useState } from "react"; const Child = memo(function Child({ onClick }) { console.log("Child rendered"); return <button onClick={onClick}>Child button</button>; }); function Parent() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); const handleClick = useCallback(() => { console.log("clicked"); }, []); // same function every time return ( <> <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>Parent: {count}</button> <Child onClick={handleClick} /> {/* does not re-render on count */} </> ); } REMEMBER: memo skips unchanged children. useCallback keeps function props stable.

Complete ReactJS Made Simple - page 14 22. Custom Hooks: Your Own Reusable Logic A custom hook is a function starting with 'use' that bundles hooks together - like saving a favourite recipe so you never rewrite it. import { useState, useEffect } from "react"; function useLocalStorage(key, initial) { const [value, setValue] = useState(() => { const saved = localStorage.getItem(key); return saved ? JSON.parse(saved) : initial; }); useEffect(() => { localStorage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify(value)); }, [key, value]); return [value, setValue]; } function useToggle(start = false) { const [on, setOn] = useState(start); return [on, () => setOn(o => !o)]; } // Use them function Settings() { const [name, setName] = useLocalStorage("name", ""); const [open, toggle] = useToggle(); return <input value={name} onChange={e => setName(e.target.value)} />; } REMEMBER: Same logic in 2 places? Complete ReactJS Made Simple - page 17 27. Global State: Redux Toolkit and Zustand When many far-apart components share data (cart, user), a global store is a central warehouse. Zustand is the lightest; Redux Toolkit is the industry standard. // ---- Zustand: npm install zustand ---- import { create } from "zustand"; const useCart = create((set) => ({ items: [], add: (item) => set((s) => ({ items: [...s.items, item] })), clear: () => set({ items: [] }), })); function CartButton() { const count = useCart((s) => s.items.length); // subscribe to a slice const add = useCart((s) => s.add); return <button onClick={() => add("Shoes")}>Cart ({count})</button>; } // ---- Redux Toolkit: npm install @reduxjs/toolkit react-redux ---- import { createSlice, configureStore } from "@reduxjs/toolkit"; const counter = createSlice({ name: "counter", initialState: { value: 0 }, reducers: { inc: (s) => { s.value += 1; } }, // "mutating" is safe here }); export

"@reduxjs/toolkit"; const counter = createSlice({ name: "counter", initialState: { value: 0 }, reducers: { inc: (s) => { s.value += 1; } }, // "mutating" is safe here }); export const store = configureStore({ reducer: { counter: counter.reducer } }); // <Provider store={store}> useSelector(s => s.counter.value) useDispatch() REMEMBER: Small app: useState/Context. Big shared state: Zustand or Redux Toolkit.

You will still see them in old projects, so know the translation. New code: use function components. import { Component } from "react"; class Counter extends Component { state = { count: 0 }; componentDidMount() { console.log("mounted"); } // = useEffect(..., []) componentDidUpdate() { console.log("updated"); } // = useEffect(...) componentWillUnmount() { console.log("bye"); } // = effect cleanup increment = () => this.setState({ count: this.state.count + 1 }); render() { return ; } } // Lifecycle story: Mount (born) -> Update (grows) -> Unmount (leaves) REMEMBER: Lifecycle: mount, update, unmount. Hooks do the same job in function components.

Performance: Why Components Re-render A component re-renders when its state changes, its props change, or its parent re-renders. Usually that is fast. Complete ReactJS Made Simple - page 26 40. Folder Structure and Best Practices Keep the project tidy like a well-organized kitchen. src/ components/ small reusable pieces (Button, Card, Modal) pages/ one file per screen (Home, Login, Dashboard) hooks/ custom hooks (useLocalStorage.js) context/ ThemeContext, AuthContext services/ API calls (api.js) utils/ helper functions assets/ images, fonts App.jsx main.jsx // Best practices // 1. One component = one job; split when a file passes ~150 lines // 2. Keep state as LOW as possible, lift only when needed // 3. Never mutate state; derive values instead of storing them // const total = items.reduce(...) // not useState for total // 4. Unique stable keys in lists // 5. Handle loading and error states // 6. Extract repeated logic into custom hooks // 7. Use ESLint + Prettier; name components in PascalCase REMEMBER: Small components, low state, derived values, custom hooks. 41. Common Mistakes

Common Mistakes to Avoid Every React beginner meets these. Spot them early! // 1. Mutating state // items.push(x); setItems(items); WRONG // setItems([...items, x]); RIGHT // 2. Infinite loop: setState inside useEffect with no deps // useEffect(() => { setCount(count + 1); }); // loops forever! // useEffect(() => { setCount(c => c + 1); }, []); // runs once // 3. Missing dependencies // useEffect(() => { fetchUser(id); }, []); // stale id! // useEffect(() => { fetchUser(id); }, [id]); // correct // 4. Calling the function instead of passing it // <button onClick={doIt()}> WRONG // <button onClick={doIt}> RIGHT // 5. Index as key in changing lists // 6. Storing derived data in state // 7. Forgetting cleanup for timers and listeners

<button onClick={doIt()}> WRONG // <button onClick={doIt}> RIGHT // 5. Index as key in changing lists // 6. Storing derived data in state // 7. Forgetting cleanup for timers and listeners // 8. Defining a component INSIDE another component (it resets every render) // 9. Reading state right after setState (it is not updated yet) REMEMBER: Replace state, add deps, pass functions, clean up effects.
